**Given:** The standard torus as a periodic smooth quotient, an irrational real number $a$, its cotangent bundle with canonical form, and the regular level $C=0$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Assume countable choice ACω, meaning every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

[F1] [[def-rpm-h-cotangent-phase-space]]: cotangent coordinates carry $\omega=dx^i\wedge dp_i$, with Hamiltonian convention $\iota_{X_C}\omega=dC$.

[F2] [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]: a regular constraint level is an embedded hypersurface; a one-constraint system is first class when its self-bracket vanishes.

[F3] [[thm-rpm-h-first-class-local-reduction]]: regular first-class constraints have local symplectic leaf spaces, with no global Hausdorff conclusion.



1.1 The periodic quotient atlas makes $T^2$ a smooth manifold. By [F1], its cotangent form is $\omega=dx\wedge dp_x+dy\wedge dp_y$. The differential $dC=dp_x+a\,dp_y$ is nowhere zero, so $C^{-1}(0)$ is a regular embedded hypersurface. The canonical bracket is skew, hence $\{C,C\}=0$ and the single constraint is first class. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra, construct]

2.1 Contraction with $dx\wedge dp_x+dy\wedge dp_y$ gives $X_C=\partial_x+a\partial_y$. Integrating this constant vector field yields the stated flow and leaves momenta fixed. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix a starting point $(x_0,y_0)$ and any target first coordinate $u\in[algebra, step 2.1]

4.1 The orbits through $(0,0,0,0)$ and $(0,1/2,0,0)$ are distinct: equality would require integers $n,k$ with $an+k=1/2$; if $n\ne0$ this would make $a$ rational, and if $n=0$ it would assert that an integer equals $1/2$. Both orbits are dense by step 3.1. Let $U$ be a saturated open subset of the constraint surface that meets the fixed-momentum torus. Its intersection with that torus is nonempty, open, and saturated. Its complement is closed and saturated; if nonempty, it contains a whole dense orbit and hence the whole torus. Therefore the intersection is the whole torus. Any quotient neighborhoods of the two distinct orbit classes have such preimages and therefore intersect, so the orbit space is non-Hausdorff. This does not contradict the local symplectic leaf spaces in [F3]. [F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The flat branch of [[def-rpm-charge-spin-model]], the adopted LAD equation in [[post-rpm-lad-effective-equation]], Minkowski signature $(-,+,+,+)$, $c>0$, $\tau_e>0$, and the constants above.

[A1] Adopt the flat LAD equation as a physical model assumption and set the prescribed external two-form to zero.

[F1] [[def-hyperbolic-functions]] and [[thm-hyperbolic-identities-and-derivatives]]: $\cosh^2\theta-\sinh^2\theta=1$ and the derivatives of $\cosh$ and $\sinh$ are $\sinh$ and $\cosh$.

[F2] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-ftc-first-part]], and [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: the displayed smooth functions differentiate by the chain/product rules, and the integral defining $x$ has derivative $U$.

[F3] [[post-rpm-lad-effective-equation]]: for $F=0$, LAD reads $a=\tau_e(\dot a-\eta(a,a)U/c^2)$.

[F4] [[lem-rpm-ll-reduced-ode]]: when $F=0$, $f_0=B=0$, so the reduced LL acceleration field vanishes.



1.1 The integral defining $x$ is well-defined on every compact $\tau$ interval because $U$ is smooth by [F2]. The fundamental theorem [F2] gives $\dot x=U$. By [F1], $\eta(U,U)=c^2(-\cosh^2\theta+\sinh^2\theta)=-c^2$. Also $U^0=c\cosh\theta>0$, so $U$ is future directed in the chosen inertial chart. Thus $\tau$ is proper time and $x$ is future timelike. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Differentiating with [F1, F2] gives $$a=c\theta'(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0),\qquad \dot a=c\theta''(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)+c(\theta')^2(\cosh\theta,\sinh\theta,0,0), \qquad \eta(a,a)=c^2(\theta')^2.$$ Consequently $\dot a-\eta(a,a)U/c^2=c\theta''(\sinh\theta,\cosh\theta,0,0)$, and the force-free equation [F3] is equivalent to $\theta'=\tau_e\theta''$. The chosen $\theta$ has $\theta'=Ae^{(\tau-\tau_0)/\tau_e}$ and $\theta''=\theta'/\tau_e$, so the equation holds identically. This proves that the curve solves the adopted LAD equation for every real proper time. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The invariant $\eta(a,a)=c^2(\theta')^2$ gives $\sqrt{\eta(a,a)}=c|A|e^{(\tau-\tau_0)/\tau_e}$, which is unbounded toward the future. For $F=0$, [F4] gives $a_{\rm LL}=0$, hence its local solutions have constant $U$. The displayed LAD solution is non-inertial since $A\ne0$, so it demonstrates that the force-free LAD equation admits runaway solutions even though the reduced LL force-free field does not. This is an ODE comparison, not an empirical conclusion. [A1, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $m>0$, $\tau_e>0$, the stated smooth compactly supported nonnegative pulse, and the separate ODE and future boundary condition above.

[A1] Adopt only for this mathematical example the scalar equation $a=F_{\rm ext}/m+\tau_e a'$ and the future decay condition.

[F1] [[thm-ftc-first-part]] and [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: a continuous integrand on each compact interval has the integral regularity needed for the fundamental theorem of calculus.

[F2] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]], [[thm-chain-rule]], and [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: exponentials differentiate by the chain rule, and products obey the product rule.

[F3] [[thm-monotonicity-of-the-integral]] and [[lem-integral-elementary-bounds]]: the integral of a nonnegative continuous function is nonnegative and bounded below by a positive lower bound times interval length.

[F4] [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]]: $e^x>0$ and $e^{-x}=1/e^x$.

[F5] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: a continuous real function on a compact interval attains its minimum; if it is positive everywhere then that minimum is positive.

[F6] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]: the mean value theorem and positive derivative give strict increase of the real exponential.

[F7] [[thm-exponential-limits-and-range]]: $e^x\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$.



1.1 Define $I(t):=\int_t^\infty e^{(t-s)/\tau_e}F_{\rm ext}(s)\,ds$, interpreting the integral as a finite Riemann integral after any upper truncation beyond $\max\{t,T\}$; compact support makes the value independent of that truncation. For $t<T$, write $I(t)=e^{t/\tau_e}\int_t^T e^{-s/\tau_e}F_{\rm ext}(s)\,ds$. By [F1] the integrand is integrable on this compact interval, and [F2] together with the fundamental theorem gives $$I'(t)=-F_{\rm ext}(t)+\frac{1}{\tau_e}I(t)\qquad (t<T).$$ For $a=I/(m\tau_e)$ this identity becomes $\tau_e a'= -F_{\rm ext}/m+a$, which rearranges to the displayed Abraham–Lorentz equation. For $t>T$, both $I$ and $F_{\rm ext}$ vanish, so the same equation holds. At $t=T$, smoothness and support imply $F_{\rm ext}(T)=0$, and the one-sided derivatives agree with the displayed identity. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For $t\geq T$, the integration interval contains no point where $F_{\rm ext}$ is nonzero, so $a(t)=0$. For $t<0$, continuity and nonnegativity of the nonzero pulse give a closed subinterval of $(0,T)$ on which $F_{\rm ext}\geq d>0$. The exponential factor is positive and continuous there by [F2, F4]; its minimum is positive by [F5]. The integral over that subinterval is strictly positive by the lower bound [F3], and all remaining contributions are nonnegative. Thus $a(t)>0$. Since $a(t)=0$ for $t\geq T$, it satisfies the future boundary condition. [given, A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, step 1.1]

3.1 If $a_1,a_2$ are two solutions, their difference $d=a_1-a_2$ satisfies $d'=d/\tau_e$. The product rule gives $(e^{-t/\tau_e}d(t))'=0$, so [F6] implies this product is a constant $C$. By [F4], $d(t)=Ce^{t/\tau_e}$; if $C\ne0$, then [F7] makes $|d(t)|\to\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$, contradicting $d(t)\to0$. Hence $C=0$ and $d=0$, proving uniqueness. Together with step 2.1, the unique future-decaying solution is strictly positive for all $t<0$: this pre-acceleration is a property of the stated model equation, not an empirical claim. [A1, F2, F4, F6, F7, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The flat LL definitions from [[lem-rpm-ll-reduced-ode]], a common compact interval, the stated $C^3$ normalized curves, fixed $C^2$ field, and all five uniform bounds.

[A1] Each curve obeys the displayed LAD equation, with $\varepsilon>0$ serving as its radiation-time parameter.

[A2] $\eta(U_\varepsilon,U_\varepsilon)=-c^2$ throughout $I$; all derivatives below are ordinary proper-time derivatives in the flat inertial chart.

[F1] [[lem-rpm-ll-reduced-ode]]: $f_0^a=\alpha F^a{}_bU^b$, $B^a=\alpha(\partial_bF^a{}_c)U^bU^c+\alpha^2F^a{}_bF^b{}_cU^c$, and $\Pi_U{}^a{}_b=\delta^a_b+U^aU_b/c^2$.

[F2] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]] and [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: differentiating $F(x(\tau))U(\tau)$ uses the coordinate product and chain rules.



1.1 Differentiating $\eta(U_\varepsilon,U_\varepsilon)=-c^2$ gives $\eta(U_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)=0$. Differentiating this identity once more gives $\eta(U_\varepsilon,\dot a_\varepsilon)=-\eta(a_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)$. By [F1], $\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}\dot a_\varepsilon=\dot a_\varepsilon+U_\varepsilon\eta(U_\varepsilon,\dot a_\varepsilon)/c^2=\dot a_\varepsilon-\eta(a_\varepsilon,a_\varepsilon)U_\varepsilon/c^2$. Therefore [A1] is exactly $a_\varepsilon=f_{0,\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}\dot a_\varepsilon$. [given, A1, A2, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The product and chain rules [F2], with $\dot x=U$ and $\dot U=a$, give $$\dot f_{0,\varepsilon}^a=\alpha_\varepsilon(\partial_bF^a{}_c)U^bU^c+\alpha_\varepsilon F^a{}_b a_\varepsilon^b, \qquad B_\varepsilon^a=\alpha_\varepsilon(\partial_bF^a{}_c)U^bU^c+\alpha_\varepsilon F^a{}_b f_{0,\varepsilon}^b.$$ Subtracting the equalities and using $\delta_\varepsilon=a_\varepsilon-f_{0,\varepsilon}$ gives $\dot f_{0,\varepsilon}-B_\varepsilon=\alpha_\varepsilon F\delta_\varepsilon$. [given, A2, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Subtract $f_{0,\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}B_\varepsilon$ from the reformulated LAD equation in step 1.1. Since $\dot a-B=\dot\delta+(\dot f_0-B)$, step 2.1 yields $$a_\varepsilon-(f_{0,\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}B_\varepsilon) =\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}(\dot\delta_\varepsilon+\alpha_\varepsilon F\delta_\varepsilon).$$ Taking Euclidean norms and applying the assumed bounds gives at each $\tau\in I$ $$\left\|a_\varepsilon-(f_{0,\varepsilon}+\varepsilon\Pi_{U_\varepsilon}B_\varepsilon)\right\| \leq\varepsilon P(C_1\varepsilon+A M C_0\varepsilon) =P(C_1+AM C_0)\varepsilon^2.$$ The constants do not depend on $\varepsilon$ or $\tau$, so the estimate is uniform on $I$. [given, A1, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** $Q$, its canonical symplectic cotangent phase space, a smooth $H$, and where used a smooth time-dependent Hamiltonian $H_t$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Assume countable choice ACω, meaning every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

[F1] [[def-rpm-h-cotangent-phase-space]]: in induced coordinates $\omega=\sum_i dq^i\wedge dp_i$; observables are smooth real functions.

[F2] [[thm-smooth-functions-form-a-poisson-algebra]]: the symplectic bracket is coordinate independent, skew, bilinear, satisfies Leibniz and Jacobi.

[F3] [[thm-smooth-dependence-of-ode-solutions-on-parameters]]: a $C^1$ locally Lipschitz vector field has unique local solutions, and a smooth vector field depending smoothly on initial data and parameters has smooth local solution dependence.



1.1 Write $X_H=A^i\partial_{q^i}+B_i\partial_{p_i}$. Contraction gives $\iota_{X_H}\omega=A^i dp_i-B_i dq^i$. Equating with $dH=H_{q^i}dq^i+H_{p_i}dp_i$ yields $A^i=H_{p_i}$, $B_i=-H_{q^i}$. [given, A1, F1, algebra]

2.1 Substitution into $X_G(F)$ gives the displayed coordinate bracket. Its intrinsic definition from ω makes the formula invariant under cotangent coordinate changes; [F2] supplies the Poisson identities. [given, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Along a solution, the chain rule gives $dF/dt=F_t+dF(X_{H_t})$; the definition of the bracket and skewness give $dF(X_{H_t})=X_{H_t}(F)=\{F,H_t\}$. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.3 Smoothness of $H_t$ makes its coordinate Hamiltonian vector field smooth. Applying [F3] on the open domain yields unique local solutions and smooth dependence wherever solutions remain in that domain. This conclusion says nothing about extension beyond that interval. [given, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For smooth autonomous $H$, $d\omega=0$ and $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$ imply $\mathcal L_{X_H}\omega=d\iota_{X_H}\omega+\iota_{X_H}d\omega=d^2H=0$; differentiating the pullback along the local flow therefore gives zero, and its initial value is ω, so the flow preserves ω. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** An open interval, a symplectic $P$, a smooth constraint family with regular slices $N_\lambda$, a smooth ambient $H_c$, and smooth multipliers.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Assume countable choice ACω, meaning every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

[F1] [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]: at each fixed parameter, the independent constraint differentials define the tangent space as the intersection of their kernels.

[F2] [[thm-rpm-h-canonical-poisson-and-flow]]: $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$, $dF(X_H)=\{F,H\}$, and the stated bracket convention applies.

[F3] [[thm-darboux-theorem]]: locally a symplectic form has canonical coordinates $\omega=dq^i\wedge dp_i$.

[F4] [[thm-cm-stationarity-iff-euler-lagrange]]: fixed-endpoint first variation of a smooth first-order action vanishes exactly when its Euler–Lagrange equations hold.



1.1 In a Darboux chart, the integrand is $p_i\dot q^i-H_c-u^a\chi_a$. Variation of $u^a$ is arbitrary and gives $\chi_a=0$; variation of each $p_i,q^i$, with endpoint variations zero, and [F4] gives Hamilton's equations for $H_T=H_c+u^a\chi_a$. [given, A1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 The multiplier functions depend on λ only, so $d_zH_T=dH_c+u^a d\chi_a$. By linearity of $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$, $X_{H_T}=X_{H_c}+u^aX_{\chi_a}$. If instead phase-dependent extensions $u^a(z,\lambda)$ are used, the extra term $\chi_aX_{u^a}$ vanishes on $N$. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Differentiate $\chi_a(\lambda,z(\lambda))=0$ along a solution; the chain rule yields $0=\partial_\lambda\chi_a+d_z\chi_a(\dot z)$. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Substitute the vector field from step 2.1 and use [F2]: $d_z\chi_a(X_{H_c})=\{\chi_a,H_c\}$ and $d_z\chi_a(X_{\chi_b})=\{\chi_a,\chi_b\}$, giving the displayed consistency equation on $N_\lambda$. Its possible algebraic outcomes depend on its coefficient matrix and remaining constraints; no rank or termination premise was assumed. [given, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A $2n$-dimensional symplectic manifold, a regular common level $N$, and constraints whose mutual brackets vanish on $N$.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: assume countable choice ACω, the exact choice strength used by the cotangent smooth-structure supplier; no full axiom of choice is assumed.

[F1] [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]: $T_zN=\cap_a\ker d\chi_a(z)$.

[F2] [[def-symplectic-form-and-symplectic-manifold]]: $\omega$ is closed and nondegenerate; $\iota_{X_f}\omega=df$.

[F3] [[def-symplectic-orthogonal-complement]]: $W^\omega=\{v:\omega(v,w)=0\text{ for all }w\in W\}$, equivalently the inverse image of the annihilator under $\omega^\flat$.

[F4] [[prop-symplectic-double-orthogonal-and-dimension-identities]]: for each tangent subspace $W$, $\dim W+\dim W^\omega=\dim P$.

[F5] [[thm-smooth-dependence-of-ode-solutions-on-parameters]]: smooth linear ODEs have unique local solutions smoothly dependent on parameters.

[F6] [[thm-frobenius-local-coordinate-theorem]]: a smooth involutive rank-$r$ distribution has local coordinates in which leaves are the $s$-coordinate slices with $y$ constant.

[F7] [[thm-rpm-h-canonical-poisson-and-flow]]: the convention is $\{F,G\}=X_G(F)$ and $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$.




1.1 For $w\in T_zN$, [F1] gives $d\chi_a(w)=0$, hence $\omega(X_{\chi_a},w)=0$ and each $X_{\chi_a}\in(T_zN)^\omega$. The $d\chi_a$ are independent, so their images under the isomorphism $\omega^\flat$ are independent; therefore these $r$ vectors are independent. The level has codimension $r$, and [F4] gives $\dim(T_zN)^\omega=r$, so they span the symplectic orthogonal. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 On $N$, $d\chi_b(X_{\chi_a})=\{\chi_b,\chi_a\}=0$ by first-classness and [F7], so each $X_{\chi_a}$ is tangent. Their independence from step 1.1 implies $r\le\dim N=2n-r$, hence $r\le n$. The radical of the restricted form is $T_zN\cap(T_zN)^\omega$; since the orthogonal is already spanned by tangent $X_{\chi_a}$, this intersection is exactly that span. [given, F1, F2, F3, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For smooth kernel fields $U,V$ and any tangent field $W$, apply $d\omega_N=0$ to $(U,V,W)$. All terms containing contractions with $U$ or $V$ vanish, leaving $\omega_N([U,V],W)=0$. Thus ([U,V]) is again in the kernel and the distribution is involutive. [given, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The Frobenius frame proof solves a transverse linear matrix ODE to straighten a local frame. Its coefficients are smooth, so [F5] gives a smooth local solution in transverse coordinates; the initial matrix is identity, so its determinant remains nonzero after shrinking the coordinate neighborhood. The resulting frame is involutive and [F6] supplies local $(s,y)$ coordinates. This explicitly supplies the parameter dependence needed in that construction. [given, F5, F6, step 3.1]

5.1 Since every $\omega_N$-kernel vector is tangent to the $s$-leaves, the contraction of $\omega_N$ with $\partial_{s^a}$ vanishes. Therefore its coordinate expression has no $ds^a$ factor. [step 2.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 For each leaf vector $U$, Cartan's identity gives $\mathcal L_U\omega_N=d\iota_U\omega_N+\iota_Ud\omega_N=0$. Thus the coefficients of the remaining $dy^i\wedge dy^j$ form are independent of $s$; they define a form $\omega_{\mathrm{red}}$ on the local $y$-space and the coordinate projection pulls it back to $\omega_N$. It is closed because $d\omega_N=0$, and nondegenerate because its kernel would lift to a vector in $TN$ orthogonal to all of $TN$, hence to the already-quotiented kernel. [given, F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** A smooth nondegenerate Lorentz metric, $c>0$, the displayed first-order functional and the selected future massive or nonzero future-null branch, and smooth curves/covectors with fixed endpoint events.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Assume countable choice ACω, meaning every sequence of nonempty sets has a choice function; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

[F1] On future-timelike smooth curves with fixed endpoint events, define the mathematical functional $S[x]=-mc\int_a^b\sqrt{-g(x\prime,x\prime)}\,d\lambda$ for fixed $m,c>0$. Its Lorentzian geometry is supplied by [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. No physical motion principle is assumed.

[F2] For $m=0$, select the stationary triples with $p\ne0$, $p^\sharp$ future null, and smooth multiplier $e>0$. This is a mathematical branch condition on the displayed first-order functional, with independent variations taken before imposing $C_0=0$.

[F3] [[thm-gr-nondegenerate-levi-civita-and-tensor-derivative]]: the metric-compatible torsion-free Levi-Civita connection exists and $\nabla g=0$.

[F4] [[def-geodesic-of-an-affine-connection]]: an affine geodesic satisfies $\nabla_{\dot x}\dot x=0$.

[F5] [[def-covariant-derivative-along-a-curve]]: covariant differentiation obeys the coordinate connection formula and product rule.

[F6] [[thm-cm-stationarity-iff-euler-lagrange]]: fixed-endpoint stationarity is equivalent to the Euler–Lagrange equations.

[F7] [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]: a regular constraint level is specified by independent differentials, and its total generator is the canonical Hamiltonian plus multiplier-weighted constraints.

[F8] [[thm-rpm-h-canonical-poisson-and-flow]]: the convention is $\iota_{X_H}\omega=dH$ and canonical Hamilton equations have the corresponding signs.

[F9] [[thm-rpm-h-homogeneous-massive-shell]]: for $m>0$ the square-root Legendre image is the embedded future mass shell with positive-ray fibres.



1.1 Use the supplied smooth tangent and cotangent bundles under [A1], with the mathematical functionals and selected branches [F1,F2]. In a spacetime chart, variation in $e$ gives $C_m=0$. Variation in $p_a$ gives $x'^a=e g^{ab}p_b$. Variation in $x^a$, integrating the $p_a\delta x'^a$ term by parts with $\delta x$ vanishing at endpoints, gives $p'_a=-e\partial_a C_m=-\tfrac e2\partial_a g^{bc}p_bp_c$. The vertical differential of $C_m$ is $d_pC_m=p^\sharp$; it is nonzero on the massive branch because $g^{-1}(p,p)=-m^2c^2<0$, and on the massless branch because $p\ne0$ and $g^{-1}$ is nondegenerate. Thus the shell is a regular primary constraint by [F7], and [F8] fixes the canonical sign convention. The equations are tensorial and hence agree across overlapping charts. [given, A1, F1, F2, F6, F7, F8, algebra]

2.1 For $m>0$, the first equation gives $p_a=g_{ab}x'^b/e$. The constraint gives $g(x',x')=-e^2m^2c^2$, so $s=\sqrt{-g(x',x')}=emc$ because $e,m,c>0$.
